C# conformance

C# that behaves like .NET in the browser

Every case below is a piece of C# run twice: on .NET, and as the JavaScript WebSharper compiles it to. The results are compared character by character. Where they differ, it is listed as a known difference, with what to write instead.

WebSharper 11 · core 24cff94d 339 cases in 8 areas as of 2026-11-25

Same result as .NET

95.0%

322 of 339 cases

Known differences

17

where JavaScript itself differs, each with an alternative

Unexplained differences

0

silent mismatches; 0 cases rejected at compile time

Known differences

WebSharper implements a .NET API in JavaScript when it can follow .NET semantics exactly or very closely. It doesn't when that would bloat small, readable output just for coverage, or when only a partial imitation is possible, such as System.Type, which cannot tell apart .NET types that share a JavaScript representation. Those cases are listed here, each with the C# or JavaScript API to use instead.

string.equality.refStrings and formatting

JavaScript strings are values: two equal strings are never different references.

Instead:Compare strings with == or string.Equals.

The case
{ var a = "ab"; var b = string.Concat("a", "b"); return B(a == b) + "," + B((object)a == (object)b) + "," + B(a.Equals(b)); }
.NETtrue,false,true
JStrue,true,true
boxing.equalityTypes and dates

Values are not boxed in JavaScript: two boxed equal numbers compare equal by reference too.

Instead:Compare unboxed values instead of relying on reference identity.

The case
{ object a = 1, b = 1; return B(a == b) + "," + B(a.Equals(b)) + "," + B(Equals(a, b)); }
.NETfalse,true,true
JStrue,true,true
float.precisionNumbers

float is a JavaScript number, so it keeps double precision instead of rounding to single.

Instead:Use double, or a Float32Array from WebSharper.JavaScript when single-precision storage matters.

The case
{ float f = 0.1f; return $"{f}|{(double)f}"; }
.NET0.1|0.10000000149011612
JS0.1|0.1
array.outofrangeCollections

Array accesses are not bounds-checked: reading past the end gives undefined instead of throwing IndexOutOfRangeException.

Instead:Check Length before indexing.

The case
{ var a = new int[2]; return $"{a[2]}"; }
.NETEXN IndexOutOfRange
JSundefined
exception.null.derefLanguage

Dereferencing null throws a JavaScript TypeError, not a NullReferenceException.

Instead:Check for null (or use ?.) instead of catching NullReferenceException.

The case
{ string s = null; return $"{s.Length}"; }
.NETEXN NullReference
JSEXN Exception
dict.insertion.orderCollections

After a Remove, .NET reuses the freed slot for the next Add; that order is unspecified in .NET, and JavaScript keeps insertion order.

Instead:Sort the keys, or use SortedDictionary, when order matters.

The case
{ var d = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["b"] = 1, ["a"] = 2, ["c"] = 3 }; d.Remove("a"); d["d"] = 4; return J(d.Keys); }
.NET[b,d,c]
JS[b,c,d]
generic.defaultTypes and dates

Generics are erased: default(T) inside generic code is null for value types too.

Instead:Pass the default value in, or constrain T to a class.

The case
$"{Box<int>.Default()}|{Box<string>.Default() ?? "null"}"
.NET0|null
JSnull|null
enum.getvaluesPattern matching

Enums are erased to numbers: a boxed or generic enum value formats as its number.

Instead:Call ToString on the statically typed enum value.

The case
J(Enum.GetValues<Color>())
.NET[Red,Green,Blue]
JS[0,5,6]
list.capacity.tostringCollections

No runtime type names: Object.ToString on a type that does not override it does not give the .NET type name.

Instead:Override ToString, or use nameof.

The case
new List<int>().ToString()
.NETSystem.Collections.Generic.List`1[System.Int32]
JS""
object.tostring.defaultTypes and dates

No runtime type names: Object.ToString on a type that does not override it does not give the .NET type name.

Instead:Override ToString, or use nameof.

The case
new Plain().ToString()
.NETConformance.Plain
JS[object Object]
gettype.nameTypes and dates

No reflection: GetType() is not available in JavaScript.

Instead:Use nameof for names, pattern matching (is) for type tests, or WebSharper.JavaScript.Object.GetPrototypeOf for the JavaScript prototype.

The case
new Dog().GetType().Name
.NETDog
JScompile error: not supported
span.sumCollections

Span<T> and stackalloc are not supported.

Instead:Use arrays, or JavaScript typed arrays from WebSharper.JavaScript.

The case
{ Span<int> s = stackalloc int[] { 1, 2, 3 }; var t = 0; foreach (var x in s) t += x; return $"{t}"; }
.NET6
JScompile error: not supported
datetime.isoTypes and dates

A DateTime has no Kind in JavaScript: the "o" format writes local time with its offset, never "Z".

Instead:Use DateTimeOffset, or Date.toISOString from WebSharper.JavaScript for a UTC timestamp.

The case
new DateTime(2024, 7, 4, 9, 3, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc).ToString("o")
.NET2024-07-04T09:03:00.0000000Z
JS2024-07-04T11:03:00.0000000+02:00
readonly.wrapperCollections

AsReadOnly returns a snapshot, not a live wrapper: it doesn't see later changes to the list.

Instead:Call AsReadOnly again after changing the list, or pass the list as IReadOnlyList<T>.

The case
{ var l = new List<int> { 1 }; var r = l.AsReadOnly(); l.Add(2); return $"{r.Count}"; }
.NET2
JS1
sorteddictionary.keys.liveCollections

SortedDictionary.Keys and .Values are snapshots, not live views: they don't see later changes.

Instead:Read Keys/Values again after changing the dictionary.

The case
{ var d = new SortedDictionary<int, string> { [1] = "a" }; var keys = d.Keys; d[2] = "b"; return $"{keys.Count}"; }
.NET2
JS1
typeof.nameTypes and dates

No reflection: System.Type is not available in JavaScript, and a partial typeof(T).Name would suggest otherwise.

Instead:Use nameof(T) for names, or WebSharper.JavaScript.Object.GetPrototypeOf for the JavaScript prototype.

The case
typeof(Dog).Name + "|" + typeof(List<int>).Name
.NETDog|List`1
JScompile error: not supported
typeof.fullnameTypes and dates

No reflection: System.Type is not available in JavaScript, and a partial typeof(T).Name would suggest otherwise.

Instead:Use nameof(T) for names, or WebSharper.JavaScript.Object.GetPrototypeOf for the JavaScript prototype.

The case
typeof(Dog).FullName + "|" + typeof(Dog).Namespace + "|" + typeof(string).FullName + "|" + typeof(Dictionary<string, int>).Name
.NETConformance.Dog|Conformance|System.String|Dictionary`2
JScompile error: not supported

How this is computed

The cases live in WebSharper's own repository (tests/WebSharper.CSharp.Conformance). The same C# project is built for .NET and with WebSharper, run on .NET and under Node, and the outputs are compared. The check runs on every release build against a committed baseline, so a change that makes any case worse fails the build. The TypeScript declarations WebSharper generates for the cases are type-checked too.

Same as .NET: JavaScript prints exactly what .NET prints.
Known difference: an accepted difference that follows from JavaScript, listed above with its alternative.
Mismatch: a different result with no accepted reason, a bug to fix.

For tools and AI agents

The results are published as JSON: every case with its C# source, its .NET output and its status, and the known differences with their reasons and alternatives.

  • /Assets/conformance/csharp.json

Whether an API translates at all is a separate question: see API coverage.

F# conformance

F# that behaves like .NET in the browser

Every case below is a piece of F# run twice: on .NET, and as the JavaScript WebSharper compiles it to. The results are compared character by character. Where they differ, it is listed as a known difference, with what to write instead.

Known differences

WebSharper implements a .NET API in JavaScript when it can follow .NET semantics exactly or very closely. It doesn't when that would bloat small, readable output just for coverage, or when only a partial imitation is possible, such as System.Type, which cannot tell apart .NET types that share a JavaScript representation. Those cases are listed here, each with the F# or JavaScript API to use instead.

float32.arithNumbers

float32 is a JavaScript number, so it keeps double precision instead of rounding to single.

Instead:Use float, or a Float32Array from WebSharper.JavaScript when single-precision storage matters.

The case
string (0.1f + 0.2f)
.NET0.3
JS0.30000000000000004
recursion.deep.nontailLanguage

JavaScript has a fixed call stack, so deep non-tail recursion overflows sooner than on .NET.

Instead:Write the function tail-recursive (WebSharper turns self tail calls into loops), or use a loop or a fold.

The case
let rec f n = if n = 0 then 0 else 1 + f (n - 1) in string (f 10000)
.NET10000
JSEXN Exception
string.equalityStrings and printf

JavaScript strings are values: two equal strings are never different references.

Instead:Compare strings with = or String.Equals.

The case
B (s "abc" = "a" + "bc") + "," + B (obj.ReferenceEquals(s "abc", "a" + s "bc"))
.NETtrue,false
JStrue,true
equals.boxedRecords, unions and equality

Numbers are not boxed with their .NET type in JavaScript: box 1 and box 1.0 are the same value.

Instead:Compare unboxed values of a known type.

The case
B ((box 1).Equals(box 1)) + "," + B ((box 1).Equals(box 1L)) + "," + B (box 1 = box 1.0)
.NETtrue,false,false
JStrue,false,true
match.typetest.float.intPattern matching

int and float are both JavaScript numbers, so :? int cannot tell a whole-number float from an int.

Instead:Keep the static type, or use a union case per numeric type.

The case
match box 2.0 with :? int -> "int" | :? float -> "float" | _ -> "?"
.NETfloat
JSint
match.typetest.char.stringPattern matching

A char is a one-character JavaScript string, so :? string also matches a boxed char.

Instead:Keep the static type, or use a union case per type.

The case
match box 'c' with :? string -> "string" | :? char -> "char" | _ -> "?"
.NETchar
JSstring
string.index.out.of.rangeStrings and printf

String indexing is not bounds-checked: reading past the end gives undefined instead of throwing IndexOutOfRangeException.

Instead:Check Length before indexing.

The case
string (s "abc").[5]
.NETEXN IndexOutOfRange
JS<null>
exception.nullrefLanguage

Dereferencing null throws a JavaScript TypeError, not a NullReferenceException.

Instead:Use options or check with isNull instead of catching NullReferenceException.

The case

JSEXN Exception
option.value.propRecords, unions and equality

None is null, so .Value on it throws a JavaScript TypeError, not a NullReferenceException.

Instead:Match on the option, or use Option.defaultValue.

The case

JSEXN Exception
dictionary.union.keyMaps, sets and dictionaries

None is null, which .NET rejects as a Dictionary key; JavaScript accepts it.

Instead:Use Map, or a key type without a null case.

A DateTime has no Kind in JavaScript: the "o" format writes local time with its offset.

Instead:Use DateTimeOffset, or Date.toISOString from WebSharper.JavaScript for a UTC timestamp.

Instead:Use nameof for names, :? patterns for type tests, or WebSharper.JavaScript.Object.GetPrototypeOf for the JavaScript prototype.

The case
(box 1).GetType().Name
.NETInt32
JScompile error: not supported
enum.parseRecords, unions and equality

No reflection: Enum.Parse takes a System.Type, which is not available in JavaScript.

Instead:Match the string against the enum's cases instead.

The case
string (Enum.Parse(typeof<Color>, "Blue") :?> Color)
.NETBlue
JScompile error: not supported
char.unicode.upperStrings and printf

JavaScript upper-cases strings with full Unicode case mapping, so String.ToUpper turns "ß" into "SS" where .NET keeps "ß".

Instead:Upper-case per character with String.map Char.ToUpper, which keeps characters that have no single-character upper case.

The case
string (Char.ToUpper 'ß') + "," + (s "straße").ToUpper()
.NETß,STRAßE
JSß,STRASSE
string.concat.nullStrings and printf

+ on strings is JavaScript string concatenation, which writes a null string as "null"; treating null as "" would add a check to every concatenation.

Instead:Pass a string that may be null through string s, which gives "" for null.

The case
s "a" + (null: string) + "b"
.NETab
JSanullb
resultRecords, unions and equality

No runtime type names: string of a Result or Choice value is the .NET type name, which JavaScript does not have.

Instead:Match on the cases and format the value inside.

The case
let r : Result<int, string> = Ok 1 in string (Result.map ((+) 1) r) + "," + string (Result.bind (fun _ -> Error "e") r : Result<int, string>)
.NETMicrosoft.FSharp.Core.FSharpResult`2[System.Int32,System.String],Microsoft.FSharp.Core.FSharpResult`2[System.Int32,System.String]
JS[object Object],[object Object]
datetime.tostringDates, math and conversions

DateTime.ToString() uses the browser's locale (toLocaleString), as .NET uses the current culture, so the text depends on where it runs (the check runs .NET with the invariant culture).

Instead:Pass a format, such as ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"), for a fixed text.

The case
string (d ())
.NET02/29/2024 13:45:30
JS2/29/2024, 1:45:30 PM

How this is computed

The cases live in WebSharper's own repository (tests/WebSharper.FSharp.Conformance). The same F# project is built for .NET and with WebSharper, run on .NET and under Node, and the outputs are compared. The check runs on every release build against a committed baseline, so a change that makes any case worse fails the build.

Same as .NET: JavaScript prints exactly what .NET prints.
Known difference: an accepted difference that follows from JavaScript, listed above with its alternative.
Mismatch: a different result with no accepted reason, a bug to fix.

For tools and AI agents

The results are published as JSON: every case with its F# source, its .NET output and its status, and the known differences with their reasons and alternatives.

  • /Assets/conformance/fsharp.json

Whether an API translates at all is a separate question: see API coverage.
